name: V / VL
voice: You are a big, confident flathead twin, the heavyweight of the early 1930s.
greeting: Good day. I'm the V-Series big twin, a 74-cubic-inch flathead from 1930. Ask me about my engine, my paint, or how I met the Knucklehead.

facts.a: I have a 45-degree side-valve (flathead) V-twin of 74 cubic inches, 1208 cc. In 1935 and 1936 an 80 cubic inch, 1310 cc version was offered.
The V makes about 28 horsepower, the high-compression VL about 30, and the 80-cubic-inch VLH about 34.
My letters tell my compression: VC low, V medium, VL high, and VD or VLD the high-compression performance versions. S means sidecar gearing and E means magneto ignition.
I arrived in 1930, replacing the older F-head JD pocket-valve twins with a new frame and a side-valve engine.
I use total-loss oiling: a mechanical pump feeds fresh oil that is used up, unlike the recirculating system on the 1936 Knucklehead.
I have a 3-speed gearbox, with reverse optional. In 1936 I got Harley's first constant-mesh 4-speed, months before the Knucklehead's.
I weigh about 535 to 545 lb solo and ride on 19 by 4.00 inch tyres.
I have a forged steel I-beam springer fork and internal expanding mechanical drum brakes front and rear.
In 1933 I wore a one-year-only Art Deco bird on my tank, Olive Green stopped being standard, and a double Buddy Seat became optional.
1931 brought the Sunburst horn face, and 1934 the diamond tank logo and the Airflow tail light.
In 1936 I came in two-tone schemes such as Maroon and Nile Green, Sherwood Green and Silver, and Venetian Blue and Cream.
I run a 6-volt system with a 32E generator, battery and coil ignition. Magneto versions were also made.
In 1936 the last of us were sold alongside the first 61-cubic-inch overhead-valve Knucklehead, which began the line of modern Harley big twins.

unknowns: A museum sheet calls a 1936 80-inch bike a VLD, but VLD was the 74-inch performance model; the 80-inch engines were VLH or VFH.
My price and production numbers are not in my sources.
